titleStmt.title: Learning to Encode Timing: Mechanisms of Plasticity in the Auditory Brainstem

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Learning to Encode Timing: Mechanisms of Plasticity in the Auditory Brainstem

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether the auditory brainstem, long treated as a hard-wired relay optimised for timing, is a site of experience-dependent plasticity
span.quote: Mechanisms of plasticity have traditionally been ascribed to higher-order sensory processing areas such as the cortex, whereas early sensory processing centers have been considered largely hard-wired. In agreement with this view, the auditory brainstem has been viewed as a nonplastic site, important for preserving temporal information and minimizing transmission delays.

span.label: does the mammalian auditory brainstem express the cellular mechanisms that could support the learning effects seen in humans
span.quote: A key question is whether the auditory brainstem in mammals expresses the mechanisms that allow activity-dependent modulation of neural circuits and that could support the learning phenomena observed in human studies.

span.label: assembles slice physiology and human evoked-potential evidence to overturn the view that early auditory processing is non-plastic, and identifies cell-specific synaptic and intrinsic plasticity in brainstem nuclei
span.quote: However, recent groundbreaking results from animal models and human studies have revealed remarkable evidence for cellular and behavioral mechanisms for learning and memory in the auditory brainstem.

span.label: existence
span.quote: However, recent groundbreaking results from animal models and human studies have revealed remarkable evidence for cellular and behavioral mechanisms for learning and memory in the auditory brainstem.

span.label: auditory brainstem plasticity
span.quote: In agreement with activity-dependent changes in human auditory brainstem evoked responses and contrary to the traditional views that early sensory processing is largely hard-wired, recent studies have revealed that the auditory brainstem is a site where robust synaptic and intrinsic plasticity take place.

span.label: review
span.quote: Contrary to traditional views that early stages of sensory processing are not plastic, new studies discussed in this article have established that the auditory brainstem is dynamic.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Synapse-specific plasticity simultaneously disinhibits fusiform cells and strengthens their excitatory input, driving the fusiform hyperactivity that underlies tinnitus
span.quote: Synapse-specific synaptic plasticity, by decreasing the activity of inhibitory interneurons (disinhibition) and simultaneously increasing excitatory input to fusiform cells, can lead to hyperactivity in fusiform cells, similar to the kind observed in animals with behavioral evidence of tinnitus.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Anti-Hebbian STDP reweights parallel-fiber synapses so that inputs predicting incoming sensory activity are weakened, building a 'negative image' that cancels the sensory consequences of the animal's own movements
span.quote: In this way, anti-Hebbian STDP adjusts parallel fiber synaptic weights in order to sculpt a “negative image” of the neural response caused by the fish’s own movements.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Nitric oxide diffusing out of MNTB principal neurons suppresses postsynaptic Kv3 channels in neighbouring cells, providing intercellular gain control during loud sound
span.quote: Diffusion of NO from MNTB principal neurons provides modulatory control of excitability via direct suppression of postsynaptic Kv3 channels

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Corticofugal (efferent) feedback from higher-order processing levels descends onto brainstem nuclei and is the route by which language and musical experience alter subcortical timing
span.quote: This finding suggests that higher-order processing levels should have efficient feedback pathways to brainstem lower-order processing levels.

span.label: the field inferred incapacity from function - a structure optimised for fast reliable signalling was assumed to be ill-suited to plasticity, and the test was not run
span.quote: Knowing that neurons in the auditory brainstem are specialized for generating fast, reliable, and consistent electrical signals, it has been assumed that the synaptic relays of auditory brainstem nuclei are ill-suited to plasticity.

span.label: and effort was directed to the cortex instead, which is where the plasticity literature accumulated
span.quote: Studies related to long-term plasticity and learning-related phenomena have focused on higher processing stages of the auditory system, such as the auditory cortex ( Schreiner and Winer, 2007 ; Fritz et al., 2007 ; Weinberger, 2007 ; Atiani et al., 2009

span.label: the reversal is built from two independent lines that meet in the middle - slice physiology in animals and non-invasive evoked potentials in humans
span.quote: Two series of observations have led to reevaluation of these views. The first is that long-term synaptic and intrinsic plasticity do occur in some auditory brainstem nuclei. Second, electrophysiological studies in humans have uncovered new forms of learning and behavioral plasticity that are mediated by auditory brainstem structures. These findings establish a new role for the auditory brainstem and its modification by experience and pathology.

span.label: adding an in-vivo-like feature to the standard slice preparation reversed a standing conclusion about the same nucleus
span.quote: Introduction of high spontaneous, in-vivo-like activity in brain slices prepared from the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB) revealed synaptic failures during high-frequency activity ( Hermann et al., 2007 ) not seen in previous studies.

span.label: and the authors generalise the warning rather than confining it to that result
span.quote: In addition these results highlight that several plasticity protocols may be modified by in-vivo-like conditions.

span.label: plasticity is shown to be feature-specific rather than a gain change, which is what makes it evidence of learning rather than of arousal
span.quote: Modification of auditory brainstem processing by language and musical experience does not result in a stimulus-independent, generalized gain effect. Instead, distinctive aspects of stimulus processing (e.g., high-frequency phase locking, onset synchrony) are impaired or enhanced depending on the behavioral relevance and relative complexity of the stimulus, likely influencing how the sensory system responds

span.label: the functional interpretation of the dorsal cochlear nucleus is imported wholesale from the electrosensory lobe of a fish, where anti-Hebbian plasticity cancels self-generated input
span.quote: In this way, anti-Hebbian STDP adjusts parallel fiber synaptic weights in order to sculpt a “negative image” of the neural response caused by the fish’s own movements.

span.label: the argument that the same job exists in audition is made by matching the problem, not the anatomy - both systems must separate external signals from self-generated ones
span.quote: Electric fish are faced with the challenge of differentiating external sensory signals (predator or prey) from self-generated “noise.” The auditory system faces a similar task in that it must differentiate spectral changes in a sound introduced by the animal’s own movements from spectral changes introduced by the movement of an external sound source relative to the animal.

span.label: human timescales are stacked deliberately: lifelong language and musical experience, then training over weeks, then attention within a session
span.quote: While language, musical training, and subcortical impairments represent lifelong experiences, brainstem processing can also be modified by shorter-term auditory training (e.g., over the course of weeks) ( Russo et al., 2005 ; Song et al., 2008 ; de Boer and Thornton, 2008

span.label: the same plasticity mechanisms are used to explain a pathology, which converts the review's claim into something testable in tinnitus
span.quote: Synapse-specific synaptic plasticity, by decreasing the activity of inhibitory interneurons (disinhibition) and simultaneously increasing excitatory input to fusiform cells, can lead to hyperactivity in fusiform cells, similar to the kind observed in animals with behavioral evidence of tinnitus.

span.label: a theory built for visual cortex is extended below the cortex, and the extension is flagged as the authors' view rather than an established result
span.quote: Because the top-down mechanism was originally proposed for the impact of higher-order visual cortical areas to lower-order cortical areas, the focus has been primarily on the intracortical feedback pathway.

span.label: The synaptic-plasticity evidence base comes overwhelmingly from brain slices, which differ substantially from the intact brain.
span.note: what this limits: every plasticity claim in the review: MOST STUDIES OF SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY IN THE AUDITORY BRAINSTEM HAVE BEEN PERFORMED IN BRAIN SLICES
span.quote: Most studies of synaptic plasticity in the auditory brainstem have been performed in brain slices.

span.label: How naturally occurring noise exposure would induce the plasticity proposed to underlie tinnitus is not established.
span.note: what this limits: the tinnitus account specifically: it is obvious that ELECTRICAL STIMULATION OF PARALLEL FIBERS CAN INDUCE SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY, but how naturally occurring noise exposure would do so is not established
span.quote: While it is obvious that electrical stimulation of parallel fibers can induce synaptic plasticity that could change the balance of excitation and inhibition in fusiform cells, it is not entirely clear how stimulation caused by noise exposure could produce similar plasticity effects.

span.label: How brainstem pathways adapt to ongoing sensory activity and contribute to perception of environmental sound remains largely unknown.
span.note: what this limits: what the brainstem literature covers: MUCH LESS IS KNOWN ABOUT HOW THESE PATHWAYS ADAPT TO ONGOING SENSORY ACTIVITY AND HOW THEY CONTRIBUTE TO THE PERCEPTION AND INTERPRETATION OF ENVIRONMENTAL SOUNDS, INCLUDING SPEECH
span.quote: This research has provided insight into how sounds are localized by vertebrates, but much less is known about how these pathways adapt to ongoing sensory activity and how they contribute to the perception and interpretation of environmental sounds, including speech, under normal and pathological conditions.

span.label: most of the plasticity evidence comes from slices, which differ from the intact brain in ways that have already changed one conclusion
span.note: what this limits: the plasticity evidence base as a whole: MOST STUDIES OF SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY IN THE AUDITORY BRAINSTEM HAVE BEEN PERFORMED IN BRAIN SLICES. THIS EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH HAS SUBSTANTIAL DIFFERENCES FROM STUDYING INTACT BRAINS IN VIVO
span.quote: Most studies of synaptic plasticity in the auditory brainstem have been performed in brain slices. This experimental approach has substantial differences from studying intact brains in vivo.

span.label: how noise exposure would induce the plasticity proposed to cause tinnitus is not established
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 1 - how naturally occurring noise exposure would induce the plasticity proposed to underlie tinnitus is not established
span.quote: While it is obvious that electrical stimulation of parallel fibers can induce synaptic plasticity that could change the balance of excitation and inhibition in fusiform cells, it is not entirely clear how stimulation caused by noise exposure could produce similar plasticity effects.

span.label: the pathophysiology of tinnitus remains poorly understood despite its prevalence
span.note: what this limits: any mechanistic claim about the disorder: DESPITE THE WIDE PREVALENCE OF TINNITUS, THE PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF THE DISORDER IS POORLY UNDERSTOOD
span.quote: Despite the wide prevalence of tinnitus, the pathophysiology of the disorder is poorly understood.

span.label: whether the fish-derived cancellation function applies to the dorsal cochlear nucleus is posed as an open question, not answered
span.note: what this limits: the transfer of the cancellation function from the fish circuit: A KEY QUESTION IS WHETHER ANTI-HEBBIAN PLASTICITY OBSERVED IN THE DCN CAN SERVE A SIMILAR FUNCTION
span.quote: A key question is whether anti-Hebbian plasticity observed in the DCN can serve a similar function.

span.label: whether brainstem plasticity is driven top-down, locally, or by both is unresolved
span.note: what this limits: the locus of control for brainstem plasticity: whether changes are INITIATED/MODULATED IN A TOP-DOWN FASHION ... OR THROUGH LOCAL MECHANISMS OF ADAPTATION is unresolved
span.quote: Whether activity-dependent changes are initiated/modulated in a top-down fashion, as predicted by the RHT through the efferent, corticofugal system linking the cortex and the auditory brainstem; through local mechanisms of adaptation to the acoustic properties of the input ( Dean et al., 2005 ); or through an interaction of afferent and efferent mechanisms is a challenge for future research to resolve.

span.label: how these pathways adapt and contribute to perception is much less understood than how they transmit timing
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 2 - transmission of timing is understood far better than adaptation or perception
span.quote: This research has provided insight into how sounds are localized by vertebrates, but much less is known about how these pathways adapt to ongoing sensory activity and how they contribute to the perception and interpretation of environmental sounds, including speech, under normal and pathological conditions.

span.label: The Reverse Hierarchy Theory, first formulated to describe top-down influence of higher visual cortical areas on lower ones, is taken over to explain top-down modulation of auditory processing and extended below cortex to the brainstem.
span.quote: Because the top-down mechanism was originally proposed for the impact of higher-order visual cortical areas to lower-order cortical areas, the focus has been primarily on the intracortical feedback pathway.

span.label: The adaptive-sensory-processor / 'negative image' account of anti-Hebbian STDP in the cerebellum-like electrosensory lobe is imported as a candidate functional model for the mammalian dorsal cochlear nucleus.
span.quote: The auditory system faces a similar task in that it must differentiate spectral changes in a sound introduced by the animal’s own movements from spectral changes introduced by the movement of an external sound source relative to the animal.

span.label: anti-Hebbian STDP building a negative image that cancels the sensory consequences of the animal's own movements, imported as the candidate function of the dorsal cochlear nucleus
span.quote: In this way, anti-Hebbian STDP adjusts parallel fiber synaptic weights in order to sculpt a “negative image” of the neural response caused by the fish’s own movements.

span.label: the Reverse Hierarchy Theory, built for higher-to-lower visual cortical areas and extended here to corticofugal control of the brainstem
span.quote: The RHT postulates that the performance of a perceptual task is first based on the highest available level of sensory representation. If the task cannot be accomplished at that level (because of poor sensory resolution), it proceeds down the representational hierarchy to obtain more detailed, lower-level cues that participate in generating the percept.

span.label: the parallel-fiber and climbing-fiber arrangement, used both as the structural analogy for the DCN and as the model for how auditory nerve activity might induce plasticity
span.quote: Cerebellum-like structures act as adaptive sensory processors in which the signals conveyed by parallel fibers in the molecular layer predict the patterns of sensory input to the deep layers through a process of associative anti-Hebbian synaptic plasticity

span.label: STDP - Hebbian at fusiform cells and anti-Hebbian at cartwheel cells; ONE induction protocol producing opposite signs, decided by cell type
span.quote: The same protocol induces LTP in fusiform cells and LTD at cartwheel cells.

span.label: the auditory brainstem - as a hard-wired relay optimised for timing versus as a plastic, experience-modified structure; the paper is the transition between the two readings
span.quote: Mechanisms of plasticity have traditionally been ascribed to higher-order sensory processing areas such as the cortex, whereas early sensory processing centers have been considered largely hard-wired. In agreement with this view, the auditory brainstem has been viewed as a nonplastic site, important for preserving temporal information and minimizing transmission delays.

span.label: plasticity - synaptic (changed connection strength) versus intrinsic (changed excitability through ion channels); the review insists a circuit needs one or the other
span.quote: Therefore, all neural circuits supporting experience-dependent plasticity display synaptic or intrinsic plasticity or both.

span.label: experience effects - as a generalised gain change versus as feature-specific alteration; only the second counts as learning
span.quote: Modification of auditory brainstem processing by language and musical experience does not result in a stimulus-independent, generalized gain effect. Instead, distinctive aspects of stimulus processing (e.g., high-frequency phase locking, onset synchrony) are impaired or enhanced depending on the behavioral relevance and relative complexity of the stimulus, likely influencing how the sensory system responds

span.label: the MNTB - as a simple faithful relay versus as a nucleus that fails under realistic activity; the reading depends on what the slice preparation includes
span.quote: This is an important finding suggesting that the MNTB is not a simple and faithful relay nucleus, and while it encodes precisely the onset of sound-like stimuli (as bursts of discharges), it may not reliably entrain to high-frequency stimuli for prolonged periods, due to short-term plasticity.

span.label: brainstem plasticity - as adaptive learning versus as the cause of a disease; the same mechanism read with opposite valence in tinnitus
span.quote: Synapse-specific synaptic plasticity, by decreasing the activity of inhibitory interneurons (disinhibition) and simultaneously increasing excitatory input to fusiform cells, can lead to hyperactivity in fusiform cells, similar to the kind observed in animals with behavioral evidence of tinnitus.

span.label: claim_type: critique
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: existence — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Contrary to traditional views that early stages of sensory processing are not plastic, new studies discussed in this article have established that the auditory brainstem is dynamic.

span.label: method: narrative review pairing rodent brain-slice recordings of synaptic and intrinsic plasticity with non-invasive human auditory brainstem responses
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: review — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Finally and most importantly, the possibility of assessing the function of auditory brainstem nuclei noninvasively in humans makes it possible to relate auditory processing in these nuclei to the performance of sensory tasks.

span.label: phenomenon: experience-dependent plasticity in subcortical auditory processing
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: auditory brainstem plasticity — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Taken together, these results suggest that sound processing in the human brainstem is dynamic and that experience-dependent plasticity results in specific alteration of receptive field properties.

span.label: extends → Reverse Hierarchy Theory (Ahissar and Hochstein, 2004)
span.quote: Therefore, it is our view that RHT may apply to subcortical sensory processing and that the application of its principles may initiate or modulate plasticity at the auditory brainstem.

span.label: contradicts → the traditional view that early sensory processing stages are hard-wired and non-plastic
span.quote: Contrary to traditional views that early stages of sensory processing are not plastic, new studies discussed in this article have established that the auditory brainstem is dynamic.

span.label: critiques → the inference from specialisation for precise timing to incapacity for plasticity
span.quote: Knowing that neurons in the auditory brainstem are specialized for generating fast, reliable, and consistent electrical signals, it has been assumed that the synaptic relays of auditory brainstem nuclei are ill-suited to plasticity.

span.label: contradicts → the treatment of the MNTB as a simple and faithful relay nucleus
span.quote: This is an important finding suggesting that the MNTB is not a simple and faithful relay nucleus, and while it encodes precisely the onset of sound-like stimuli (as bursts of discharges), it may not reliably entrain to high-frequency stimuli for prolonged periods, due to short-term plasticity.

span.label: builds-on → Krishnan and colleagues, who first showed that language experience alters brainstem pitch encoding
span.quote: Krishnan and colleagues were the first to demonstrate that language experience affects brainstem activity by showing that speakers of tonal languages have enhanced neural representation of pitch ( Krishnan et al., 2005

span.label: extends → the Reverse Hierarchy Theory, from intracortical feedback to subcortical processing
span.quote: Because the top-down mechanism was originally proposed for the impact of higher-order visual cortical areas to lower-order cortical areas, the focus has been primarily on the intracortical feedback pathway.

span.label: supports → the account of tinnitus as centrally maintained rather than purely cochlear
span.quote: Synapse-specific synaptic plasticity, by decreasing the activity of inhibitory interneurons (disinhibition) and simultaneously increasing excitatory input to fusiform cells, can lead to hyperactivity in fusiform cells, similar to the kind observed in animals with behavioral evidence of tinnitus.

span.label: Hebbian —contrasted-with→ anti-Hebbian
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: In contrast, parallel fiber-cartwheel cell synapses are characterized by an anti-Hebbian timing rule. Presynaptic inputs that reliably cause, or predict, a postsynaptic spike are weakened and therefore LTD is observed when postsynaptic spikes follow EPSPs ( Figure 3 ) ( Bell et al., 1997

span.label: fusiform —contrasted-with→ cartwheel cells
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: The same protocol induces LTP in fusiform cells and LTD at cartwheel cells.

span.label: RETRACTED (WRONG TYPE: a KIND, not a PART) · intrinsic plasticity —part-of→ plasticity
span.note: RETRACTED: WRONG TYPE: a KIND, not a PART. Intrinsic plasticity is a sort of plasticity, not a component of it. — strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: Therefore, all neural circuits supporting experience-dependent plasticity display synaptic or intrinsic plasticity or both.

span.label: frequency following response —part-of→ auditory brainstem response
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: The frequency following response (FFR), a component of the ABR that occurs in response to a periodic stimulus, is well suited for examining how speech elements are encoded subcortically

span.label: plasticity —causes→ tinnitus
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.75
span.quote: Synapse-specific synaptic plasticity, by decreasing the activity of inhibitory interneurons (disinhibition) and simultaneously increasing excitatory input to fusiform cells, can lead to hyperactivity in fusiform cells, similar to the kind observed in animals with behavioral evidence of tinnitus.

span.label: Kv3.1b —causes→ intrinsic plasticity
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: At low levels of sound intensity (quiet environment), phosphorylation of Kv3.1b by protein kinase C (PKC) reduces potassium current, thus allowing low-frequency firing. Conversely, in response to high-frequency auditory or synaptic stimulation, channel dephosphorylation and increased Kv3.1b channel promote the ability of neurons to fire at high frequency ( Song et al., 2005

span.label: spike-timing-dependent plasticity —part-of→ long-term potentiation
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85
span.quote: STDP observed at parallel fiber-fusiform cell synapses is Hebbian ( Figure 3 ) and resembles STDP timing rules observed in the cortex and hippocampus ( Caporale and Dan, 2008 ). At these synapses, presynaptic inputs that are successful in driving postsynaptic spikes are strengthened; therefore, LTP is observed when postsynaptic spikes follow excitatory postsynaptic potentials

span.label: dorsal cochlear nucleus —part-of→ auditory brainstem
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: Recent studies of the dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN), an auditory brainstem nucleus bearing significant resemblance to the cerebellum

span.label: musicians —causes→ auditory brainstem
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85
span.quote: Musical experience can also result in more robust brainstem encoding of speech sounds, linguistic pitch-patterns, and processing of vocal expressions of emotion ( Figure 1 , middle and bottom panels, Musacchia et al., 2007 ; Wong et al., 2007

span.label: intrinsic plasticity —is-a→ plasticity
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — RETYPED from part-of. 'all neural circuits ... display synaptic OR intrinsic plasticity or both' lists KINDS of plasticity. NO kindhood cue is present, so this edge stands on the compound name and is marked accordingly - the type is my reading, not the text's.
span.quote: Therefore, all neural circuits supporting experience-dependent plasticity display synaptic or intrinsic plasticity or both.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: These studies have demonstrated unique, opposing forms of spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) at parallel fiber synapses onto fusiform and cartwheel cells. Error bars report ±SEM.

span.label: fast Fourier transform
span.quote: The frequency following response (FFR), a component of the ABR that occurs in response to a periodic stimulus, is well suited for examining how speech elements are encoded subcortically

span.label: phase locking
span.quote: The frequency following response (FFR), a component of the ABR that occurs in response to a periodic stimulus, is well suited for examining how speech elements are encoded subcortically

span.label: The auditory brainstem, traditionally regarded as hard-wired, is in fact dynamic and expresses experience-dependent plasticity.
span.quote: Contrary to traditional views that early stages of sensory processing are not plastic, new studies discussed in this article have established that the auditory brainstem is dynamic.

span.label: In the dorsal cochlear nucleus one and the same spike-pairing protocol strengthens parallel-fiber synapses onto fusiform cells (LTP, Hebbian) while weakening those onto cartwheel cells (LTD, anti-Hebbian), so the plasticity rule is cell-specific rather than nucleus-wide.
span.quote: The same protocol induces LTP in fusiform cells and LTD at cartwheel cells.

span.label: Language experience reshapes brainstem coding: speakers of tonal languages show enhanced neural representation of pitch.
span.quote: Krishnan and colleagues were the first to demonstrate that language experience affects brainstem activity by showing that speakers of tonal languages have enhanced neural representation of pitch

span.label: Experience-driven changes in the brainstem are selective to particular stimulus features rather than an across-the-board amplification of all responses.
span.quote: Modification of auditory brainstem processing by language and musical experience does not result in a stimulus-independent, generalized gain effect.

span.label: Acoustic environment tunes intrinsic excitability: in quiet conditions PKC phosphorylation of Kv3.1b potassium channels lowers the potassium current so that neurons fire only at low frequencies.
span.quote: At low levels of sound intensity (quiet environment), phosphorylation of Kv3.1b by protein kinase C (PKC) reduces potassium current, thus allowing low-frequency firing.

span.label: The medial nucleus of the trapezoid body is not a faithful relay: under in-vivo-like spontaneous activity it fails to entrain reliably to prolonged high-frequency stimuli because of short-term plasticity, even though it still encodes stimulus onset precisely.
span.quote: This is an important finding suggesting that the MNTB is not a simple and faithful relay nucleus, and while it encodes precisely the onset of sound-like stimuli (as bursts of discharges), it may not reliably entrain to high-frequency stimuli for prolonged periods, due to short-term plasticity.

span.label: The authors argue that the Reverse Hierarchy Theory, formulated for cortex, extends to subcortical processing and may itself initiate or modulate brainstem plasticity.
span.quote: Therefore, it is our view that RHT may apply to subcortical sensory processing and that the application of its principles may initiate or modulate plasticity at the auditory brainstem.

span.label: one induction protocol produces LTP in fusiform cells and LTD in cartwheel cells, so the sign of plasticity is set by cell type
span.quote: The same protocol induces LTP in fusiform cells and LTD at cartwheel cells.

span.label: speakers of tonal languages have enhanced neural representation of pitch in the brainstem
span.quote: Krishnan and colleagues were the first to demonstrate that language experience affects brainstem activity by showing that speakers of tonal languages have enhanced neural representation of pitch ( Krishnan et al., 2005

span.label: musical experience produces more robust brainstem encoding of speech, linguistic pitch patterns and vocal emotion
span.quote: Musical experience can also result in more robust brainstem encoding of speech sounds, linguistic pitch-patterns, and processing of vocal expressions of emotion ( Figure 1 , middle and bottom panels, Musacchia et al., 2007 ; Wong et al., 2007

span.label: brainstem encoding is disrupted in subsets of poor readers and children with autism
span.quote: Conversely, distinct aspects of brainstem encoding are disrupted in a subset of children with language impairment (e.g., poor readers, children with autism) ( Figure 1 , middle and bottom panels, Cunningham et al., 2001 ; Banai et al., 2009 ; Russo et al., 2008

span.label: brainstem responses are affected by attention and are larger to a speech syllable than to its time-reversed version
span.quote: Galbraith recognized the dynamic nature of the human brainstem response over a decade ago, finding that responses were affected by attention ( Galbraith et al., 1998 ) and were larger to a speech syllable than to its time-reversed version

span.label: experience does not produce a generalised gain change but alters specific stimulus features
span.quote: Modification of auditory brainstem processing by language and musical experience does not result in a stimulus-independent, generalized gain effect. Instead, distinctive aspects of stimulus processing (e.g., high-frequency phase locking, onset synchrony) are impaired or enhanced depending on the behavioral relevance and relative complexity of the stimulus, likely influencing how the sensory system responds

span.label: brainstem processing can also be changed by auditory training over weeks, not only by lifelong experience
span.quote: While language, musical training, and subcortical impairments represent lifelong experiences, brainstem processing can also be modified by shorter-term auditory training (e.g., over the course of weeks) ( Russo et al., 2005 ; Song et al., 2008 ; de Boer and Thornton, 2008

span.label: adding in-vivo-like spontaneous activity to MNTB slices revealed synaptic failures at high frequency that earlier studies had not seen
span.quote: Introduction of high spontaneous, in-vivo-like activity in brain slices prepared from the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB) revealed synaptic failures during high-frequency activity ( Hermann et al., 2007 ) not seen in previous studies.

span.label: so the MNTB is not a simple faithful relay and may not entrain reliably to sustained high-frequency input
span.quote: This is an important finding suggesting that the MNTB is not a simple and faithful relay nucleus, and while it encodes precisely the onset of sound-like stimuli (as bursts of discharges), it may not reliably entrain to high-frequency stimuli for prolonged periods, due to short-term plasticity.

span.label: phosphorylation state of Kv3.1b channels sets whether neurons fire at low or high frequency, tracking the acoustic environment
span.quote: At low levels of sound intensity (quiet environment), phosphorylation of Kv3.1b by protein kinase C (PKC) reduces potassium current, thus allowing low-frequency firing. Conversely, in response to high-frequency auditory or synaptic stimulation, channel dephosphorylation and increased Kv3.1b channel promote the ability of neurons to fire at high frequency ( Song et al., 2005

span.label: nitric oxide from one MNTB neuron modulates the excitability of its neighbours, a candidate gain control for loud environments
span.quote: activity in one MNTB neuron can modulate the excitability of adjacent neurons, suggesting that this modulation can serve as a homeostatic function for gain reduction during loud noise conditions.

span.label: retrograde GABA signalling in the lateral superior olive adjusts the excitation-inhibition balance underlying sound localisation
span.quote: For example, recent studies in the lateral superior olive (LSO) indicate that retrograde GABA signaling adjusts sound localization by balancing excitation and inhibition in the brainstem

span.label: cannabinoid receptors involved in DCN plasticity are downregulated in animals with behavioural evidence of tinnitus
span.quote: Synapse-specific synaptic plasticity, by decreasing the activity of inhibitory interneurons (disinhibition) and simultaneously increasing excitatory input to fusiform cells, can lead to hyperactivity in fusiform cells, similar to the kind observed in animals with behavioral evidence of tinnitus.

span.label: cortical activation shapes the tuning of cochlear nucleus neurons, giving a route for top-down control
span.quote: Recent findings indicate that cortical activation shapes the tuning properties of neurons in the cochlear nucleus ( Luo et al., 2008 ) similar to intra-cortical, experience-dependent shaping of receptive fields observed in primary auditory cortex ( Schreiner and Winer, 2007 ; Fritz et al., 2007 ; Atiani et al., 2009

span.label: intrinsic plasticity
span.quote: In addition to these synaptic changes, recent data provide evidence that many learning tasks and artificial patterns of activation in brain slices produce long-lasting changes in intrinsic neuronal excitability by changing the function of voltage-gated ion channels, a process called intrinsic plasticity

span.label: spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP)
span.quote: Over the last decade, studies in spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), a more physiological form of synaptic plasticity where the size and sign of plasticity depends on the relative timing of presynaptic and postsynaptic action potentials, have revealed physiologically relevant differences in synaptic plasticity timing rules in many brain areas

span.label: auditory brainstem response (ABR)
span.quote: The auditory brainstem response (ABR) is a noninvasive measure of far-field representation of stimulus-locked, synchronous electrical events.

span.label: frequency following response (FFR)
span.quote: The frequency following response (FFR), a component of the ABR that occurs in response to a periodic stimulus, is well suited for examining how speech elements are encoded subcortically

span.label: tinnitus
span.quote: Tinnitus—commonly referred to as ringing in the ears or “brain”—is the persistent perception of sound in the absence of an environmental acoustic stimulus and most often is the result of extreme sound exposure.

span.label: pitch tracking
span.quote: By analyzing the brainstem response over small time bins, we can measure the precision with which brainstem nuclei phase-lock to the time-varying pitch of the stimulus, a phenomenon known as pitch tracking.

span.label: Reverse Hierarchy Theory (RHT)
span.quote: The RHT postulates that the performance of a perceptual task is first based on the highest available level of sensory representation.

span.label: auditory brainstem response
span.quote: The auditory brainstem response (ABR) is a noninvasive measure of far-field representation of stimulus-locked, synchronous electrical events.

span.label: frequency following response

span.label: Tinnitus
span.quote: Tinnitus—commonly referred to as ringing in the ears or “brain”—is the persistent perception of sound in the absence of an environmental acoustic stimulus and most often is the result of extreme sound exposure.

span.label: Reverse Hierarchy Theory
span.quote: The RHT postulates that the performance of a perceptual task is first based on the highest available level of sensory representation. If the task cannot be accomplished at that level (because of poor sensory resolution), it proceeds down the representational hierarchy to obtain more detailed, lower-level cues that participate in generating the percept.
